newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Shots fired as Albania protesters, police clash.
newsitem.headline: Shots fired as Albania protesters, police clash.

text.p: Albanian protesters hurled hundreds of stones at riot police who fired live rounds into the air to disperse an angry crowd in the worst violence the capital has seen since popular unrest erupted last month.

Truckloads of police, supported by plain-clothes security forces, moved in with truncheons and randomly hit protesters, pushing back a crowd of about 1,000 people which attempted to push back into the city centre after an anti-government demonstration in the suburbs had ended.
A police cordon trying to hold them back gave way and the protesters came up against riot police. Rocks were thrown and then riot police began throwing stones at the protesters.
Witnesses counted at least four people who were bleeding, either from stones or being hit by police batons.
"Why did you hit us? How much did (President Sali) Berisha pay you? You should defend the people not thieves," screamed one old woman caught up in the fray.
About an hour after the clashes, police had again taken control and the situation in the capital returned to calm, but security forces kept a high profile around town.

Earlier, some 7,000 protesters demonstrated peacefully at a soccer field outside Tirana against the government's handling of the collapse of a series of pyramid schemes which wiped out the savings of thousands of Albanians.

Penniless investors blame the right-wing government of President Sali Berisha and his ruling Democratic Party for not regulating the schemes which have blossomed in Europe's poorest nation since it emerged from almost half a century of Stalinist isolation in December 1990.
"We are here to demand not only our money back but also all those years the government stole from us," Neritan Ceka, leader of the opposition Democratic Alliance party, told the crowd.
Demonstrators observed a minute's silence for Artur Rustemi who was killed during clashes with police in the southern town of Vlore ten days ago.
A group of 60 students went on hunger strike in Vlore to demand the government's resignation and full compensation for losses caused by the failure of two local funds.
In central Tirana, Berisha addressed a rally of some 5,000 party faithfuls, part of his carefully scripted week-long campaign to win back popular support.
Throughout the day, thousands of desperate investors swarmed around the country's biggest holding company after it offered to refund money to thousands of small investors.
From the early hours more than 2,000 people pushed and shoved at the iron fence around the main payout office of the Vefa Holding company, which froze all accounts last month.
But despite pledges by Vefa, which controls 80,000 accounts, investors were pessimistic that they would ever see their money again.
"The others lied to us and they're lying to us, too. They have all the money inside but they won't give it to us," said Besa Topi, who worked illegally in Greece to save money.
Vefa, a household name which boasts 240 businesses, froze client accounts after five fraudulent pyramid schemes failed last month, fearing panic withdrawals.
Topi said she had sold her apartment and invested $16,000 with Vefa and her son invested $16,000 with the fraudulent Sude scheme which has collapsed and left no assets for distribution.
"The government said it would help people who lost their homes but no one will talk to us. When we show up they send out bodyguards to drive us off," she added.

The pyramid scandal has posed the most serious crisis to date for Berisha's government, elected on a free-market ticket in 1992. He is now faced with the dilemma of printing money to appease investors, risking severe damage to the emerging market economy, or holding firm and risking more social unrest.
